extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent practitioners, policymakers, and biotech industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of U.S. patent subject-matter eligibility as applied to genes and biological inventions, synthesizing Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Le Roy, Funk Bros., Chakrabarty, Mayo, Alice, Myriad) and empirical studies on Myriad's aftermath. Aimed at evaluating legal standards and policy impacts on investment, research, and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-of-principle-to-specific-context (Le Roy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that applies an abstract principle to a specific context may be patent-eligible; historically the Court required only that abstract principles be applied to something specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically (19th century) courts accepted that carrying a principle into effect, even by simple means, could satisfy patent eligibility—i.e., application of the principle to a concrete context was sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / law-of-nature exclusion (Funk Bros.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim attempting to patent a law of nature or a naturally occurring phenomenon is ineligible if the patentee merely claims the natural principle or a limited application of it without adding an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funk Bros. invalidated a patent on a natural bacterial mixture, reasoning the patentee was claiming knowledge from the 'storehouse of knowledge of all men' and that limited application of a law of nature is insufficient for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-concept requirement for abstract ideas (Flook)
rubrics_metrics.description: An algorithm or abstract idea is not patentable absent some 'inventive concept' in its application—mere implementation of an algorithm does not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parker v. Flook struck down a patent that applied a mathematical algorithm to set a temperature alarm because it lacked an inventive concept in the application; patentees must show something more than routine application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation requirement (Diehr)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that applies an algorithm or abstract idea may be patent-eligible if it is applied in a way that transforms the claim's subject into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v. Diehr upheld a patent where the use of an algorithm in a device transformed a physical process (molded rubber production), showing that concrete application that effects transformation can satisfy eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anything-made-by-man standard (Chakrabarty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man-made organisms or products that do not occur in nature can fall outside the natural-product exclusion and be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Diamond v. Chakrabarty the Court found a genetically engineered bacterium patentable because it did not occur in nature and emphasized a broad reading of patentable subject matter: 'anything under the sun that is made by man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2001 guidance on isolated DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's Utility Examination Guidelines (2001) treated genetic sequences isolated from their natural environment as patentable subject matter, while noting sequences with no known function may fail the usefulness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO concluded that isolating DNA renders it a nonnaturally occurring product for patent purposes, though usefulness (function) remains required for utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step inventive-step test for excluded categories
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas courts must determine whether the claimed invention transforms the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application by adding an 'inventive concept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo held that merely restating a natural law and saying 'apply it' is insufficient; Alice reiterated and formalized that mere application of an abstract idea without additional inventive features fails eligibility. Courts ask whether the claim adds something significantly more to the ineligible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated DNA as naturally occurring (Myriad)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated genomic DNA sequences remain naturally occurring in their informational identity; separation from surrounding genetic material is not an act of invention and thus isolated genomic DNA is not patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court in Myriad emphasized DNA's dual nature (chemical composition and carrier of information) and held that isolating a gene does not change its defining genetic information; consequently claims to isolated genomic sequences are within the laws-of-nature exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA patent-eligibility carve-out (Myriad)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complementary DNA (cDNA), as a synthetically created molecule not naturally occurring, can be patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court in Myriad distinguished cDNA from isolated genomic DNA, holding cDNA patentable because it is not naturally occurring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to mental processes / sequence comparison are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effectively cover the mental process of comparing genetic sequences or other abstract analysis are likely ineligible absent additional inventive steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court (and affirmed aspects of the Federal Circuit) treated claims covering comparison/analysis of BRCA sequences as mental processes analogous to abstract ideas (drawing on Diehr and Flook), and the Supreme Court viewed such claims skeptically absent transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical metric — investor willingness / VC investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of Myriad's impact should measure changes in investor behavior: willingness to invest, shifts of investments away from biotech, and changes in VC funding growth rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys and VC data (e.g., Taylor, Hoyt, Schultz) measure investor perceptions and market share; findings reported reduced willingness to invest in biotech post-Myriad/Mayo/Alice and slower growth relative to other sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical metric — patent application volume and examiner behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate post-Myriad effects by analyzing USPTO application rates, rejection rates, and examiner behavior in affected fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies (e.g., Kesan & Wang) found lower application rates and higher rejection rates at the USPTO after Myriad/Mayo/Alice, disproportionately affecting biotech; such metrics indicate changes in patenting incentives and prosecution burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical metric — abandonment of development projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether patents' invalidation leads to abandonment of specific research or therapeutic development projects due to inability to secure investment without patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies (e.g., Mambalgin-1, abandoned diagnostics) provide anecdotal evidence that loss of patent prospects can lead to project termination and lost commercialization opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical metric — follow-on innovation and research use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether gene patents suppress follow-on innovation by tracking subsequent academic and commercial uses of patented genes and whether follow-on work infringes existing patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sampat & Williams, Freilich & Shahshahani found most follow-on innovations did not infringe and patenting had limited suppressive effect; these studies suggest licensing and noninfringing activity often facilitate follow-on research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer cost vs technological progress consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating policy outcomes, distinguish cost reductions due to invalidating patents (competition) from cost reductions driven by technological advances in sequencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad may have contributed to lower consumer prices for BRCA testing, but large decreases in genome sequencing costs stem largely from technological advances; attribution requires careful empirical separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-evaluation criterion — balancing industry competitiveness vs access and public-interest concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for or against restoring gene patentability require weighing effects on investment, innovation, industry competitiveness, national security, and access to diagnostics and care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents argue Myriad reduced biotech investment and competitiveness and urge legislative or doctrinal fixes; opponents point to increased access, lower testing costs, and civil-rights concerns. Policymaking should be evidence-based using the empirical metrics above.
